Writing a book requires time, patience, and many late hours of work. I am grateful for the

grow, and share knowledge with others.
– Eduardo Sojo
Contributors
About the author
Eduardo Sojo is a technology professional and solution architect with more than two decades
of experience in software development, data platforms, and artificial intelligence solutions.
Throughout his career, he has worked across multiple layers of the technology stack—from
building desktop and web applications to designing large-scale data platforms and AI-
powered systems.
Eduardo spent 14 years at Microsoft, where he worked closely with enterprise organizations to
design and implement cloud-based data and analytics solutions using Azure. During this time,
he helped customers modernize their data architectures, adopt advanced analytics, and
integrate artificial intelligence capabilities into their business processes.
He currently works as a Solution Architect at Databricks, where he focuses on helping
organizations build modern data platforms using the lakehouse architecture and leveraging
artificial intelligence and machine learning to generate value from their data. His work
frequently involves integrating enterprise data systems with modern AI technologies such as
large language models and generative AI applications.
Over the course of his career, Eduardo has worked with organizations across multiple
industries to design scalable data platforms and implement AI-driven solutions, including
computer vision, text recognition, and generative AI applications. His professional focus lies in
bridging the gap between data platforms and AI-powered applications, helping organizations
move from experimentation to production-ready AI systems.
Through this book, Eduardo shares practical insights drawn from real-world experience
designing modern data and AI solutions. His goal is to help developers, data professionals, and
architects understand how to build reliable and responsible AI applications using Microsoft
Foundry and modern enterprise data platforms.
Eduardo was born in Caracas, Venezuela, and currently lives in San Jose, Costa Rica. He enjoys
learning about new technologies, reading psychological thrillers, and spending time with his
family.
About the reviewer
Anjik Chowdhury is a senior data scientist/machine learning engineer with extensive
experience in machine learning, forecasting, and generative AI. He has built complex AI
systems across prediction, optimization, and intelligent automation, creating widespread
organizational impact. His work spans multimodal intelligence, recommendation engines, and
large-scale model deployment on cloud infrastructure. Anjik holds a master's degree in

Preface
Artificial intelligence has rapidly evolved from experimental technology into a core capability
for modern organizations. However, building real AI applications involves more than calling a
model API. Teams must manage data, select and deploy models, design prompts and
workflows, evaluate responses, monitor system behavior, and ensure that applications follow
responsible AI practices. Microsoft Foundry provides a unified platform where developers and
data professionals can build, evaluate, and deploy AI-powered solutions using generative AI
technologies.
This book provides a practical introduction to designing and implementing AI applications
using Microsoft Foundry and its new unified portal experience. Throughout the chapters, you
will learn how to work with data, deploy and orchestrate models, design AI workflows using
Prompt Flow, evaluate and monitor AI applications, and implement responsible AI safeguards.
The book also explores how AI systems can integrate with modern enterprise data platforms
such as Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks, enabling organizations to combine generative
AI with their existing data ecosystems.
This book is intended for developers, AI engineers, solution architects, and data professionals
who want to build AI solutions using Microsoft Foundry. Whether you are exploring generative
AI for the first time or looking to operationalize AI systems within an enterprise environment,
this guide will help you understand the tools and practices required to design reliable and
scalable AI applications.
Throughout the book, examples prioritize hands-on configuration using the Microsoft
Foundry portal, allowing you to understand how AI solutions are built directly within the
platform. When code is required, examples primarily use Python to demonstrate how
workflows and integrations can be extended programmatically.
Many of the concepts and practices presented in this book are based on real-world experience
designing data and AI solutions in enterprise environments. The goal is to help you move
beyond experimentation and build AI applications that are scalable, observable, and aligned
with responsible AI practices.
I have been working with Data and AI for a while with different technologies. During my time
working at Microsoft, I met many customers in different industries with necessities for
improving their data usage and looking to accelerate this journey by implementing artificial
intelligence. Working now at Databricks, I have focused on the Financial Services industry,
where AI has become a critical piece for accelerating innovation and time to market.

To get the most out of this book
To follow along with the examples presented in this book, you should have access to an Azure
subscription and familiarity with basic cloud concepts. Some examples include Python
snippets, so a basic understanding of Python and REST APIs can also be helpful.
While the book focuses primarily on using the Microsoft Foundry portal, experimenting with
the examples and adapting them to your own scenarios will help you gain a deeper
understanding of how AI systems behave in real-world environments.
Download the example code files
The code bundle for the book is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/PacktPublishing/
Microsoft-Foundry-in-Action. We also have other code bundles from our rich catalog of
books and videos available at https://github.com/PacktPublishing. Check them out!
Download the color images
We also provide a PDF file that has color images of the screenshots/diagrams used in this book.
You can download it here: https://packt.link/gbp/9781835888681.
Conventions used
There are a number of text conventions used throughout this book.
CodeInText: Indicates code words in text, database table names, folder names, filenames, file
extensions, pathnames, dummy URLs, user input, and Twitter handles. For example: "Let's
create a new resource group called rg ‑ mfddemo ‑ 01."

→ If risk > threshold

Bold: Indicates a new term, an important word, or words that you see on the screen. For
instance, words in menus or dialog boxes appear in the text like this. For example: "The
Operate section allows us to control and manage the assets created in the platform."

simplifies the development of modern AI applications. You will see that Microsoft Foundry
provides a unified environment where developers and data professionals can design, test,
evaluate, and deploy AI-powered solutions using large language models and other AI services.
You will learn how the Microsoft Foundry portal centralizes the tools required to build AI
solutions and how its components work together to support the entire AI development
lifecycle.
By the end of this part, you will have a clear understanding of the platform's architecture, core
capabilities, and how it enables teams to build and manage AI applications more efficiently.
This part of the book includes the following chapters:

Introduction to Microsoft
Foundry
With the increasing use of generative artificial intelligence in various types of applications,
techniques, and frameworks, the best practices and tools for implementing this type of
solution have also grown. Microsoft Foundry is Microsoft's response to address this need—a
unified platform to build, customize, and deploy generative AI applications in a secure and
responsible manner.
In this chapter, we will gain a thorough understanding of Microsoft Foundry, including its key
features and functionalities. We will also cover a step-by-step process for deploying Microsoft
Foundry, ensuring a smooth setup and integration. By the end of this chapter, you will have
acquired practical knowledge of how to start using it effectively, from initial setup to
leveraging its capabilities for various applications.
As such, we will cover the following main topics in the chapter:
Getting an overview of Microsoft Foundry
Deploying Microsoft Foundry
Getting started with using Microsoft Foundry

Getting an overview of Microsoft Foundry
Microsoft Foundry idx_cf5485c9idx_0324213b consists of a web portal that resides at https://ai.azure.com and requires
a valid user to have access to the different features. In it, users can develop AI applications
using pre-existing AI models in the Model Catalog, which contains several known models
such as GPT-5, DALL·E 3, Llama 4, Mistral, Cohere Command R+, Phi-4, DeepSeek-VL, and
others. It also comes with integration with other AI services that let users add additional
capabilities to their applications, like speech recognition, language and translation, vision, and
document capabilities.
Like most of the Azure services deployed, there is a section inside the Microsoft Azure portal
where additional tasks like networking, monitoring, access control, and events can be
configured. For secure enterprise environments, Foundry now supports VNet Injection and
Private Link access to restrict data movement.

important for understanding how it works in terms of architecture, roles, and other related

The architecture
In the current Microsoft Foundry idx_be0dbb38idx_c4403c81 architecture, the workflow is organized into two distinct
layers: the Foundry Resource and Foundry Projects. The top-level Foundry Resource acts as
your central control plane; this is where you handle heavy-lifting idx_50b68e99idx_a31e0184 administrative tasks like
networking (VNets), managed identities, security policies, and shared connections to AI
services. Think of it as your governance backbone. Below that, projects serve as specialized,
isolated workspaces where the actual engineering happens. Within a project, your team can
develop multi-agent workflows, fine-tune models, and manage assets like indexes and
evaluations without messing with the underlying infrastructure. This setup allows you to scale
AI development rapidly while ensuring that enterprise-grade guardrails—established at the
resource level—are automatically inherited by every project. The following image idx_d2c7ba2cidx_c17922fb helps
visualize this architecture:
5 Introduction to Microsoft Foundry
Figure 1.1: Microsoft Foundry architecture
Let's review each part of this architecture:
Two layers, one hierarchy: The Foundry Resource sits on top as the control plane;
Projects live underneath as the actual workspaces where engineering happens
The resource is your governance backbone: Set up VNets, managed identities,
security policies, and shared AI connections once — these are the heavy enterprise
concerns you don't want each team to resolve
Projects are isolated sandboxes: Each project is scoped to a specific workload (agents,
fine-tuning, retrieval), so teams move fast without stepping on each other's
infrastructure.
Inheritance is automatic: Anything you configure at the Resource level — networking
rules, identity, allowed AI endpoints — flows down to every project. No copy-paste, no
drift.

agents. When you provision a Foundry resource, specific built-in roles allow you to delegate

Summary
Let's recap. In this chapter, we introduced Microsoft Foundry as Microsoft's unified platform
for building, customizing, deploying, and managing generative AI applications in Azure. We
reviewed how Microsoft Foundry provides access to a dedicated portal, a model catalog with
popular foundation models, and integrations with Azure AI services such as speech, language,
translation, vision, and document intelligence capabilities.
We also explored the core architecture of Microsoft Foundry, focusing on the relationship
between a Foundry resource and its associated projects. The Foundry resource acts as the
central administrative layer where platform-level settings, such as networking, managed
identity, security policies, and shared service connections, are managed. Projects provide

governance and configuration defined at the resource level.
In addition, we reviewed the role-based access model used in Microsoft Foundry and discussed
how different roles support administration, project management, development, and read-only
access. We also looked at the Azure services commonly used alongside Microsoft Foundry,
including Storage Accounts, Key Vault, Application Insights, Log Analytics, Azure Container
Registry, Azure AI Search, Azure Monitor, and networking services such as Virtual Network and
Private Link.
Finally, we walked through the process of deploying a Microsoft Foundry resource from the
Azure portal, including configuring basic details, storage-related settings, networking, identity,
and encryption. We then reviewed how to access the deployed resource and open the Microsoft
Foundry portal to view the default project, inspect project information, and begin managing
users, endpoints, and related resources.
In the next chapter, we will explore the Microsoft Foundry portal in more depth and begin
working with the components used to build, configure, and evaluate AI applications.

Delving Deeper into Microsoft
Foundry's Features
In the previous chapter, you learned the basics of Microsoft Foundry, completed the initial
setup, and organized the necessary components like Projects and their associated resources to
start your AI development journey. Now it's time to dive deeper into what you can do inside
the portal and prepare your environment for building your first AI application.
The Microsoft Foundry portal is the central interface where you can manage every stage of your
AI solution, from model selection to deployment, through a collection of sections designed to
support each step of the process. The portal navigation has been streamlined into top-level
areas such as Home, Discover, Build, Operate, and Docs, making it easier to move between
development, testing, and operational monitoring.
In this chapter, we'll explore the project areas of the portal and what you can expect while
developing and implementing an AI application. We'll also look at how to adjust settings to
customize your project and manage the resources attached to it. And, we'll discuss cost
considerations that can help you plan and sustain your AI workloads.
You'll also see where newly added capabilities — such as Microsoft Foundry Agent Service for
orchestrating multi-step AI tasks, workflow-based routing for sending requests to different
models, and the Observability dashboard for monitoring performance and usage — fit into
your workflow.
We will cover these under two main headings:
Exploring Projects in the portal
Looking at the cost considerations
•
•
Technical requirements
To get the most out of this chapter, you should meet the technical requirements from Chapter 1,
including having the Azure components deployed and accessible. These will be your
foundation for experimenting with the advanced features we're about to explore.
Exploring Projects in the portal
Once Microsoft Foundry is deployed, you can access the portal at https://ai.azure.com.

chapter, we will focus on the sections most relevant to building and managing AI applications:

Models
Microsoft Foundry offers over 11,200 models for you to choose from and deploy. On this page,
you can explore all the models idx_8d7bd87d and use various filters to tailor the list to your requirements.
Some of the available filters include Collections, Capabilities, Source, Inference tasks, and

Build
This section is idx_6dc0278b where you develop and test your AI applications. You idx_ee6df1ec can experiment with
different models and configurations, and evaluate performance before deploying to
production.
Agents
An agent in Microsoft Foundry is idx_d772651f an AI program that can work independently to complete
multi-step tasks. Unlike a simple chatbot that responds to one question at a time, an agent can
reason about what to do next, use tools to gather information, and take action without waiting
for human approval on each step.
27 Delving Deeper into Microsoft Foundry's Features
Figure 2.5: Agents in the Build section
But when would you actually use idx_995210a2 an agent? Here are practical examples where agents solve real
problems:
Customer support agent: Customer emails a question, agent searches your knowledge
base, then looks up the customer account in your database, creates a ticket if needed,
and sends a personalized response. All automatically.
Data analyst agent: Employee uploads a spreadsheet, agent analyses the data, runs
calculations, generates a chart, and sends a summary email. One prompt, multiple
steps done.
IT help desk agent: Employee submits a support ticket, agent checks if it's a known
issue, runs diagnostic commands, consults your knowledge base, and escalates to a
human if needed.
Workflows
A workflow in Microsoft idx_67afc0dd Foundry is a visual way to connect multiple AI steps together without
writing code. Think of it as "drawing" the process your AI application should follow. Each step
can be a model call, a decision point, calling an external service, or running some logic.

You can use workflows for different types of scenarios, such as the following:

Email processing: When a customer email arrives, the workflow can classify it by
category, route it to the appropriate team, fill in a response template, send the reply,
and log the interaction. This follows a defined process rather than relying on a thinking
agent to decide each step dynamically.
Data transformation pipeline: When raw data arrives, the workflow can clean and
validate it, transform it into a format suitable for analysis, save it to a database, and
send a notification when the process is complete. This makes the process predictable,
repeatable, and easier to monitor.
Multi-model routing: When a question arrives, the workflow can check its complexity
and route simple questions to a faster, lower-cost model while sending more complex
questions to a more powerful model such as GPT-4o. The workflow can also log
metrics, helping teams track performance, quality, and cost over time.
Models
In this page, you have idx_39491498 access to all models deployed in the project, not only large language
models (LLM), but also AI Services and Batch Jobs.

Figure 2.7: Models in the Build section
You can deploy base models by clicking on the Deploy base model button or fine-tuned
models by clicking on the Deploy fine-tuned model button. In the AI Services tab, you can
choose between different options and start configuring them in the playground available for
each service. For Batch Jobs, you idx_d5e785d6 can see deployed jobs or create a new job. These jobs let you
manage through the Azure Open AI service high-volume processing with cost-effectiveness
and efficiency. You can create a job by clicking the Create batch job button.
It is important to know that not all the models available support global batch jobs. You can
check the latest models supported by reviewing the official documentation at https://
learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-foundry/openai/how-to/batch?view=foundry.
Fine-tuning
Fine-tuning customizes a idx_4a15a907 model for your specific use case. You do not always need it—
consider fine-tuning when prompts alone are not producing the results you need, when you
want the model to follow a very specific response style, or when you want to reduce the
amount of instruction you include in every prompt.
31 Delving Deeper into Microsoft Foundry's Features
As shown in Figure 2.8, the fine-tuning page lets you configure the basic details for a fine-
tuning job. You can select the base model, choose the customization method, and define the
training type. In this example, the selected model is gpt ‑ 4.1, the customization method is
Supervised, and the training type is Global. You also need to select a training data source, and
optionally provide validation data to test how well the fine-tuned model performs during
training.
Figure 2.8: Fine-tune in the Build section
The page also includes options such as adding a suffix to identify the fine-tuned model and
automatically deploying the idx_7f64ca2b model after the job completes. The dataset preview area on the
right shows the training data once it has been selected. If no dataset has been added yet, the
preview remains empty. This setup helps you prepare, review, and launch fine-tuning jobs
directly from the Microsoft Foundry portal.
Tools
The Tools section in the idx_76eee1ac Build area lets you add and configure external tools that your agents or
AI applications can use during execution. As shown in Figure 2.9, the catalog includes
connectors for services, such as Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure
Databricks Genie, and Azure Managed Redis, among others.

These tools can be filtered by type, provider, category, registry, and supported authentication
method, making idx_b5bc1c3b it easier to find the right integration for your project. Many of the available
tools are based on the MCP, with both local and remote MCP options shown in the catalog,
allowing your AI application to securely interact with external databases, search systems,
analytics platforms, project management tools, and deployment services.
Knowledge
The Knowledge section stores all knowledge bases and indexes from your Azure AI Search
resources. These knowledge bases idx_46a283f0 can contain documents, product information, support
content, policies, or other data that your AI application needs to retrieve while responding to
user queries.
33 Delving Deeper into Microsoft Foundry's Features
Figure 2.10: Knowledge (Foundry IQ) in the Build section
Microsoft Foundry IQ is a knowledge layer that improves how your AI retrieves information
from these indexes, making it easier to build and maintain RAG pipelines. By connecting your
project to relevant knowledge sources, you can help agents and AI applications generate
responses that are grounded in your own data rather than relying only on the model's general
knowledge.
This section is especially useful when your application needs access to current, organization-
specific, or domain-specific idx_9410559d information. For example, you can use it to support customer
service assistants, internal knowledge bots, or applications that need to search indexed
documents before generating a response.
Data
The Data section displays the idx_7c3bb117 datasets and files available in your project. These files can be
used as inputs for tasks such as fine-tuning, testing, and evaluation. From this section, you can
upload supported file types (such as .txt, .pdf, and .md) and use them as reference material for
generating data.
You can also generate synthetic data for testing and supervised fine-tuning jobs. For example,
using Simple Q&A data generation, you can create question-and-answer samples based on a
reference file. As shown in the following figure, you need to select the task type, choose the
question type, upload the reference file, set the maximum number of samples, and select the
generator model that will process the file.

The form also allows you to split the generated data into training and validation sets, which is
useful when idx_0d969692 preparing data for fine-tuning. Finally, you can specify an output file name so that
the generated dataset is saved in your project and can be reused later in the AI development

Evaluations
The Evaluations section lets you create and run evaluations to measure the quality, safety, and
performance of your AI idx_af11f971 applications. You can use evaluations to compare different agents,
models, prompts, or datasets and choose the best option based on your application
requirements. When creating an evaluation, you define the target to be evaluated, such as an
agent, model, or dataset, select the data to use, and specify the criteria or metrics that should
be measured.
35 Delving Deeper into Microsoft Foundry's Features
You can also use the Evaluator catalog, which contains ready-made evaluators for common
scenarios. As shown in Figure 2.12, the catalog includes built-in evaluators for areas such as
safety, quality, and agent behavior. Examples include evaluators for hate and unfairness, code
vulnerability, cross-model comparison, label/model comparison, rouge score, meteor score,
similarity, F1 score, document retrieval, and bleu score. These evaluators help you test your AI
application against established metrics without needing to build every evaluation from
scratch.
Figure 2.12: Evaluation in the Build section
This section is useful throughout the development lifecycle because it gives you a structured
way to validate whether your AI application is behaving as expected. By running evaluations
regularly, you idx_0b86f20f can identify weak responses, compare model outputs, measure retrieval quality,
and check whether safety requirements are being met before moving your application into
production.
Guardrails
The Guardrails section lets idx_de4f73ed you define safety and security rules for your AI applications and
agents. You can use default guardrails or create custom ones based on the risks you want to
manage. As shown in Figure 2.13, guardrails can be applied to specific model deployments or
agents, allowing you to control where each guardrail policy is enforced.

Chapter 2 36
Figure 2.13: Guardrails in the Build section
Guardrails help reduce safety and security risks by checking inputs and outputs against
configured rules. For idx_1f361d31 example, a guardrail can include checks for jailbreak attempts, content
safety risks, and protected material. The screenshot also shows a Microsoft Default V2
guardrail applied to model deployments, with categories such as jailbreak, content safety, and
protected materials available for review.
You can also create blocklists to prevent specific terms or patterns from being used in prompts.
These blocklists can match exact terms or use regular expressions, which gives you more
control over the type of content that should be blocked. Overall, this section helps you apply
consistent safety policies across your agents and models so users can interact with your AI
applications more confidently.
Until now, we've idx_2c9f7c83 explored each section of Microsoft Foundry separately. But in a real project,
these components work together as a coordinated system. Let's walk through a complete
example to see how everything connects.
The scenario: Building an AI support assistant
Imagine you're building an AI-powered customer support system. Your goal is to automate
responses to common idx_9ffee477 support questions, escalate complex issues to humans, and track
everything for compliance. When you build an agent, here's what actually happens when a
customer asks a question:
Customer: "Can I get a refund for order #12345?" 1.
37 Delving Deeper into Microsoft Foundry's Features
Question → Your deployed model reads it
Model → Queries the knowledge index for refund FAQs
Index → Returns: "Refunds available within 30 days"
Agent → Calls the CRM tool to check order date: order is 8 days old (eligible)
Agent → Consults guardrail: "Refunds under $50 approved automatically, over $50
need manager"
Agent → Orders $45, so auto-approves with: "Yes, I can process a refund. Processing
now..."
Workflow → Logs the transaction
Operate → Tracking shows one more successful refund
Customer → Gets their refund
Each component performs a specific task for your AI application; that's why all of them are
relevant when we are building agents and workflows.
Now that we have explored the Build section and seen how agents, workflows, models, tools,
knowledge sources, data, evaluations, and guardrails work together, the next step is to
understand how these assets are managed after they are created. Building an AI application is
only part of the process; you also need visibility into usage, cost, performance, compliance,
quota limits, and project administration. This is where the Operate section becomes
important. It provides a centralized area idx_4e240862 for monitoring deployed assets, reviewing operational
metrics, managing policies and guardrails, tracking quota consumption, and administering

Operate
The Operate section allows us to control and manage the assets created in the platform,
including compliance idx_17f6aa5e rules, resource quotas, and project administration. It idx_c15f2306 starts with the
Overview dashboard with the following cards:
Running agents: It shows the number of agents running versus the total number of
agents we have deployed
Estimated cost: This is the estimated cost of agents executed for the subscription and
projects in the selected period
Agent access rate: It shows in percentage the access to the agents in comparison with
the previous period
Token usage: Number of consumed tokens for models in the subscription and projects
in the selected period
Active alerts: In case of alerts present for the resources, they will be shown in this card
